title: Draft: RFC: dfilter: Allow one level of recursion with display filters
description:
Add a recursive filter syntax of the form:

    with expr1 as name1,...,exprN as nameN then principal_expr

This is a limited form of recursion (just one level) that allows
the principal filter expression to reference values from the
protocol trees that match the recursive filters. A complete
example is

    with tcp.stream == 2 as stream2 then udp.port == @{stream2:tcp.port}

or in plain english

    Filter for UDP packets with any UDP port matching any TCP port in any packet for TCP stream 2

The @{} syntax is the way to refer to a "recursive reference".
It takes a named filter and a proto field separated by a colon.

The implementation is straightforward, during dissection we inspect
and store in the runtime the values that match the reference in the
runtime (tcp.port for frames matching stream2 in this case). The fvalues
are deduplicated but this can still be a lot of data for large captures
so the performance and memory requirements need to be investigated
better.

The implementation requires a minimum of three data structures, a map
containing the recursive filters, a map of filter names to hfinfos and
a map to store the collected values, keyed by filter_name:prot0_field.

Fixes #16606.

added 1 commit
  • 86bca01d - Draft: dfilter: Allow one level of recursion with display filters
[Compare with previous version](/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/10420/diffs?diff_id=662925288&start_sha=46b60205cb55c33831531b1c798dfb6d268f0539)

The basic idea does satisfy the request. I've done a small amount of testing on [this file](/uploads/07f5cf04046fce09b5ea90d6f8202399/GTPC.cap.gz).

In GTPv1, the request has the IMSI but the response does not. They do have matching sequence numbers, and a response will have a FT_FRAMENUM field that has the frame number of a matched request. A theoretical task might be: "Show me all the requests and any responses for a given IMSI."

Some possible filter ideas (ignoring that in practice some of these might be less efficient, especially the third):

* `with e212.imsi == 228810345678903 as myimsi then e212.imsi == 228810345678903 or gtp.response_to == @{myimsi:frame.number}`
* `with e212.imsi == 228810345678903 as myimsi then gtp.seq_number == @{myimsi:gtp.seq_number}`
* `with e212.imsi == 228810345678903 as myimsi then e212.imsi == @{myimsi:e212.imsi} or gtp.response_to == @{myimsi:frame.number}`

Of these, the first one works, showing two requests (frames 5, 20605) and two paired responses (6, 20845). However, the second one only shows the two responses, and the third one shows the responses and second request (but not the first request).

That seems like a slight misfire of something that's trying to prevent an infinite loop. A frame is not matching the recursive filter if it's the frame that added the value to the recursive filter. Deduplication affects it; that is, on the second filter frames 5 and 20605 both contribute unique `gtp.seq_number` values and neither of them match, but on the third filter frame 5 contributes the imsi but 20605's is removed from deduplication.

Thanks for testing it, I will look into the remaining bugs.

It's a neat feature but I would like to have a good use case behind it to merge. I think the second one you presented is the strongest so far. It's something that wouldn't otherwise be possible (without adding generated fields to the dissector to track request and response) and should generalize to other protocols with a similar structure.

Also maybe it could be implemented somewhat differently, like ref counting the dissected protocol trees and keeping them around, or other ways I haven't thought of yet. The important thing to me is that stepping into this direction (using recursion or whatever one wants to call it) maintains a strong architectural design to support it.
Another important box that this ticks is that you only pay for what you use, that is, there is no space or time penalty for regular filters without "with" clauses.

Another variation that could be useful for some people, "show me all the frames that share field X with a set of frames":

* `with frame.number in {2, 5, 7} as myframes then gtp.seq_number == @{myframes:gtp.seq_number}`

That parses, but it has the same issue as the second one above, so it only matches the frames in the set if written as:
* `with frame.number in {2, 5, 7} as myframes then frame.number in {2, 5, 7} or gtp.seq_number == @{myframes:gtp.seq_number}`

And similarly, if you've marked a set of frames with the GUI:

`with frame.marked == TRUE as myframes then gtp.seq_number == @{myframes:gtp.seq_number}`

seems like something possibly of interest.

changed title from **Draft: dfilter: Allow one level of recursion with display filters** to **Draft: {+RFC: +}dfilter: Allow one level of recursion with display filters**

I just tried it and it seems to be pretty slow when the recursive reference has many hits. For example with capture file containing 112810 packets, the filter
`with usbll.pid == IN as in_tokens then frame.number - 1 == @{in_tokens:frame.number} and usbll.pid != DATA0`
takes 6 minutes 35 seconds to compute (`usbll.pid == IN` computers in about a second and yields 22560 hits).

The filter above is really problem specific and its idea is to show all timeouts (the capture contains only isochronous INs which always reply with DATA0). For this specific case it feels that extending usbll dissector with either an expert info and/or generated field would be much better solution.
Thanks for testing, the feedback is really appreciated.
This was interesting as a proof of concept but I don´t want to merge it. It's just not good enough as is. I think it could be more usable and elegant with multi-capture support.

commits_data.message:
Draft: dfilter: Allow one level of recursion with display filters

Add a recursive filter syntax of the form:

    with expr1 as name1,...,exprN as nameN then principal_expr

This is a limited form of recursion (just one level) that allows
the principal filter expression to reference values from the
protocol trees that match the recursive filters. A complete
example is

    with tcp.stream == 2 as stream2 then udp.port == @{stream2:tcp.port}

or in plain english

    Filter for UDP packets with any UDP port matching any TCP port in any packet for TCP stream 2

The @{} syntax is the notation for a "recursive reference".
It takes a named filter and a proto field separated by a colon.

This implementation uses two filter passes, one to collect all
the reference values (tcp.port for frames matching stream2 in this
case) and another to match the principal filter. The fvalues
are deduplicated but this can still be a lot of data for large captures
so the performance and memory requirements need to be investigated
better.

The implementation requires a minimum of three data structures, a map
containing the recursive filters, a map of filter names to hfinfos and
a map to store the collected values, keyed by filter_name:proto_field.

Fixes #16606.
